claims.text: Polycrystalline copper can exhibit temperature-dependent plastic deformation.
The temperature dependence of plastic deformation in polycrystalline copper is caused by thermally activated dislocation motion.
The proposed copper has a grain size of 10 micrometers.
The proposed copper has a random crystallographic texture.
The proposed copper has an impurity content below 0.01 wt.%.
The material will be evaluated by uniaxial tensile testing at varying temperatures.
Testing will cover 300–800 K at a constant strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.
Dislocation density and mobility mediate the temperature-dependent deformation response.
Plastic deformation proceeds through thermally activated dislocation glide and climb.
Grain-boundary sliding may assist deformation at higher temperatures.
The yield stress at 300 K is predicted to be 20% higher than at 800 K.
The stated yield-stress change is from 200 MPa to 240 MPa.
Flow stress is predicted to decrease by 15 MPa for every 100 K increase in temperature.
The baseline yield stress of polycrystalline copper at 300 K is 200 MPa.
Actual yield and flow stresses may vary with microstructure and impurity content.
Grain-boundary sliding is expected to be secondary to thermally activated dislocation motion.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome describes a 20% increase from 200 MPa to 240 MPa at 300 K relative to 800 K, implying 240 MPa at 300 K, while the baseline explicitly assigns 200 MPa to 300 K.
A decrease of 15 MPa per 100 K over the 500 K interval from 300 to 800 K implies a 75 MPa difference, which is inconsistent with the stated 40 MPa difference between 200 and 240 MPa.
